[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] Digital Realty is a publicly traded data center real estate investment trust. This session sourced two acquisitions that explain building names appearing across this operators rows in this registry. Per Data Center Dynamics trade press, Digital Realty completed a 7.8 billion dollar all-stock merger with DuPont Fabros Technology on September 15, 2017, adding 12 facilities concentrated in Ashburn, Virginia, which is why several Ashburn buildings in this registry still carry DuPont Fabros own ACC, meaning Ashburn Corporate Campus, naming convention. Separately, per Data Center Knowledge trade press, Digital Realty acquired the East Coast data center operations of AboveNet Inc. on October 2, 2006, for 40 million dollars, including a leased facility at 8100 Boone Boulevard, Vienna, Virginia, which is this registrys 8100 Boone Boulevard row. This specific row, Digital Realty Building A, matches a Baxtel campus table entry for this operators Loudoun Ashburn Campus giving 43915 Devin Shafron Drive, Ashburn, VA, distinct from the neighboring Building B through F entries on the same street and the Building G, H, J, and K entries on the separate Digital Loudoun Plaza street.

reading.body:
Digital Realty's Building A sits within the operator's multi-gigawatt Northern Virginia campus in Loudoun County, one of the largest colocation complexes in Data Center Alley. The operator publishes approximately 600 MW of IT load across its Loudoun County facilities as of 2023, but does not publish a building-specific capacity figure for Building A itself, so its individual contribution to the campus or the region cannot be determined from available data.

Virginia has 326 mapped data center facilities, of which 23 publish power capacity totaling 1375 MW. Digital Realty's Loudoun County campus ranks 24th among all published capacity in the state, meaning it accounts for a meaningful share of Virginia's announced AI-scale infrastructure but does not dominate the state's total. The gap between mapped facilities and those with published figures reflects a broader opacity in the industry about individual facility scale.

The data center colocation model constrains what Building A can tell us about AI deployment. Colocation facilities host multiple tenants with confidential workloads, so published power figures do not reveal whether a building is running AI training, inference, traditional enterprise load, or cryptocurrency mining. The facility's IT load could support thousands of accelerator cards if configured for AI training, but the operator's specification page does not confirm this use or rule it out.
